          "text": "# Perseus A: A Quiet Pinprick with a Restless Heart\n\n*At the center of the Perseus Cluster, NGC 1275 gives visual observers a faint target\u2014and astronomers a window on an active galactic nucleus.*\n\nOn a clear winter evening, Perseus rides high in the northern sky. Its brightest stars make a familiar zigzag, but the prize in this region is far less showy: a small, faint galaxy called NGC 1275, also known as Perseus A. In an eyepiece it may look like little more than a smudge. Yet this galaxy is anything but quiet.\n\nNGC 1275 is classified as a cD galaxy\u2014a large, luminous type often found near the centers of galaxy clusters\u2014and as a blazar, an especially active kind of galactic nucleus. Those labels hint at two scales of activity: a galaxy occupying a central place in its surroundings, and a compact core releasing energy. Astronomers associate such active nuclei with matter falling toward a supermassive black hole. The light we see from the galaxy\u2019s core is only one part of its story; radio observations reveal why it is known as Perseus A.\n\nThe galaxy\u2019s recorded redshift is about 0.0168, according to the SIMBAD astronomical database. Redshift describes how much the universe\u2019s expansion has stretched light on its journey to us. It is a clue astronomers use to study objects beyond our own Milky Way\u2014not something an observer can detect by eye at the telescope. SIMBAD also gives NGC 1275\u2019s J2000 coordinates as right ascension 3 hours 19 minutes 48 seconds and declination +41 degrees 30 minutes.
